query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled short-duration thermal annealing treatment near 750°C will induce the in‐situ formation of coherent, nano‐precipitates (enriched in Mn, Ni, or Si) along grain boundaries, which arrest crack propagation and enhance mechanical integrity without substantially affecting the caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: Monolithic MnNiSi0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy known for its large caloric effect but poor fracture toughness and a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal annealing treatment at approximately 750°C for a short duration (e.g., 10 minutes) followed by rapid cooling to promote nano‐precipitate formation.
generation.conditions: Test under applied magnetic fields or pressure fields within the standard operational temperature ranges for caloric performance and under compressive loading regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanometer-scale precipitates that form along grain boundaries in the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The nano‐precipitates act as localized crack deflection sites and barriers to crack propagation. Their coherent nature minimizes disruption to the caloric phase transition mechanism, allowing the alloy to retain most of its large caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement of at least ~50% in compressive strength and overall integrity compared to the untreated alloy, while retaining at least ~90% of the original caloric performance.
generation.baseline: The untreated MnNiSi0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which shows excellent caloric response but suffers from poor mechanical integrity (prone to cracking).
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected under controlled field-induced (magnetic or pressure) caloric operating conditions and under compressive (but not necessarily tensile) loading. The thermal treatment parameters (temperature, duration) must remain narrowly controlled to avoid overaging that could reduce the caloric performance.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in strength and any potential minor reductions in the caloric effect are uncertain and may require optimization of the annealing time and temperature. Additionally, the stability of the nano‐precipitates under long-term cycling remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the MnNiSi0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy: one set in the as-cast condition and one set subjected to the proposed annealing treatment (750°C for 10 minutes followed by rapid quenching). Under identical applied-field and pressure-field conditions, perform compressive mechanical tests and measure the caloric response (e.g., temperature change under applied field).
measurements: Quantitative caloric effect (e.g., ΔT per unit field)
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM or SEM) to confirm nano‐precipitate formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (target ≥50% increase) in mechanical integrity while retaining at least 90% of the caloric response compared to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.
